notes.short: They promise “freedom” while they are slaves
notes.about: Peter sets the freedom the false teachers promise against what they are themselves: slaves to depravity. Their own bondage shows how empty the promise is, for “a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.”

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity.
figure.means: the freedom the false teachers offer, set against the bondage to sin they live in themselves

notes.evidence: Bullinger (Figures of Speech) lists the verse under Antithesis: the liberty they promise against their being servants of corruption. Calvin says Peter shows their inconsistency, promising liberty while serving sin. Barnes calls them slaves of corrupt passions, themselves strangers to freedom. Clarke says their own conduct showed their system false, as they were slaves to lust.
notes.limit: The writers describe the freedom offered in different ways: from what was called needless restraint, or from the fear or yoke of God's law, leaving the hearer free to give in to lust. One also leaves open other readings, such as freedom from Roman rule.

cites.quote: “While they promise them (i.e. their dupes) liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: He shews their inconsistency, that they falsely promised liberty, while they themselves served sin, and were in the worst bondage; for no one can give what he has not. … The name of liberty is sweet, and they abused it for this end, that the hearer, being loosed from the fear of the divine law, might abandon himself unto unbridled licentiousness.

the particular liberty which these persons seem to have promised, was freedom from what they regarded as needless restraint, or from strict and narrow views of religion. … They are the slaves of gross and corrupt passions, themselves utter strangers to freedom, and bound in the chains of servitude.

cites.quote: Either to live in the highest degrees of spiritual good, or a freedom from the Roman yoke; or from the yoke of the law, or what they might term needless restraints. Their own conduct showed the falsity of their system; for they were slaves to every disgraceful lust.

notes.short: The dog and the washed sow: two old sayings
notes.about: Peter applies two common sayings to those who escaped the corruption of the world and then went back to it (verses 20 and 21): a dog returns to its vomit, and a washed sow to the mud. The first is found in Proverbs 26:11.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: A dog returns to its vomit,” and, “A sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud
figure.means: those who had escaped their old sins going back to them, as the dog and the sow go back to their filth

original.note: In Peter's Greek the word rendered “proverbs” is paroimia, a common saying, as if heard along the road; it gives this figure its old name.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia among proverbs quoted as already in use, and sets the washed sow against the stray sheep of 1 Peter 2:25. Calvin says Peter quotes two ancient proverbs, the first a saying of Solomon, and reads the purging and the washing as the gospel's work. Barnes: they went back to their former vile life. Clarke: a true proverb, of one taking up what he had left.
notes.limit: The writers differ on those who turn back: two read the washed sow as an outward reform that never changed the heart, one as a true fall from grace.

cites.at: Parœmia; or, Proverb: quoted as being already in use as such, p. 757
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such ... When we contrast this with 1Pe 2:25 , we see how forcible is the difference between the saved sinner and the “reformed character.” The saint may go astray, and the ungodly may reform ... There is all the difference in the world between a dirty sheep and a washed sow!

cites.quote: he quotes two ancient proverbs, the first of which is found as the saying of Solomon ... the gospel is a medicine which purges us by wholesome vomiting, but that there are many dogs who swallow again what they have vomited ... the gospel is also a laver which cleanses all our uncleanness, but that there are many swine who, immediately after washing, roll themselves again in the mud.

The meaning of the proverbs here quoted is, that they have returned to their former vile manner of life. Under all the appearances of reformation, still their evil nature remained, as really as that of the dog or the swine, and that nature finally prevailed.

cites.quote: This is called a true proverb: for it is a fact that a dog will eat up his own vomit; and the swine, howsoever carefully washed, will again wallow in the mire. ... But he is here represented as taking up again what he had before rejected, and defiling himself in that from which he had been cleansed. Here is a sad proof of the possibility of falling from grace
